steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key Differences Between DNA and RNA

1. Chemical Composition  
• Sugar  
  – DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
  – RNA: Ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
• Nitrogenous Bases  
  – DNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T).  
  – RNA: A, G, C, Uracil (U) instead of T.  
• Phosphate group  
  – Present in both, linking sugars via phosphodiester bonds.  
  – The extra 2′-OH in RNA makes its backbone more reactive and less stable.

2. Structure  
• DNA: Usually double-stranded, forming a long, stable double helix (B-form the most common). The strands are antiparallel and complementary.  
• RNA: Usually single-stranded. Can fold back on itself to create hairpins, loops, and complex 3-D shapes (e.g., tRNA, rRNA). Some viruses do have double-stranded RNA genomes.

3. Stability  
• DNA: Chemically and enzymatically more stable (lacks 2′-OH; protected by histones in cells). Suitable for long-term genetic storage.  
• RNA: More prone to hydrolysis and to attack by ubiquitous RNases. Designed for transient, short-lived roles.

4. Cellular Roles  
• DNA: Permanent repository of hereditary information; template for replication and transcription.  
• RNA: Functional versatility—
  – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries genetic code to ribosomes.  
  – Transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids during translation.  
  – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): core of ribosome’s catalytic activity.  
  – Regulatory/Structural RNAs: miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, snRNA, etc.  
  – Some RNAs are catalytic (ribozymes).

5. Location  
• Eukaryotes  
  – DNA: Mostly confined to nucleus (also mitochondria and chloroplasts).  
  – RNA: Synthesized in nucleus but functions mainly in cytoplasm; some in nucleolus, organelles.  
• Prokaryotes: Both are in the cytoplasm/nucleoid region.

6. Replication vs. Transcription  
• DNA self-replicates (semiconservative replication) before cell division.  
• RNA is synthesized from DNA by transcription; it does not self-replicate (except in some RNA viruses).

7. Function in Viruses  
• DNA viruses use DNA as genetic material; RNA viruses use RNA, often replicated by RNA-dependent RNA polymerases; retroviruses reverse-transcribe RNA into DNA.

8. Mutation/Fidelity  
• DNA polymerases have proofreading, giving low mutation rates.  
• RNA polymerases (cellular and viral) lack extensive proofreading, leading to higher mutation rates—useful for regulatory flexibility but less fidelity.

9. Length & Quantity  
• DNA molecules are very long chromosomes (millions to billions of bases).  
• Individual RNA molecules are typically much shorter (tens to thousands of bases), though some viral RNAs can be ~30 kb.

10. Experimental Handling  
• DNA is easier to work with (less degradation); RNA work requires rigorous RNase-free conditions.

In summary, DNA is the stable, double-stranded, long-term genetic archive; RNA is the versatile, generally single-stranded, short-lived working copy or functional molecule that decodes, regulates, and sometimes catalyzes cellular processes.
